title: Polynomial-time classical algorithms for mean-field models up to the glass transition
abstract: The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model is a strongly interacting fermionic system that has been well-studied in condensed matter and high energy physics. It is highly quantum: Gaussian states are far from the thermal state (Hastings and O'Donnell, STOC'22) and representing the thermal state requires large polynomial-size quantum circuits (Anschuetz et al., QIP'25). Very recently, it was nonetheless proven that classical algorithms can estimate local thermal expectations at sufficiently high temperature in quasipolynomial time (Zlokapa, FOCS'26). We show that classical algorithms can in fact estimate local observables at all constant temperatures in polynomial time. Our techniques also extend straightforwardly to classical systems: we resolve an open question about computing thermal expectations of a classical spin glass up to its phase transition (Bencs et al., STOC'26). Our proof develops a fully rigorous quantum cavity method. Due to the success of the classical cavity method in optimization, sampling, inference and learning, we expect the quantum cavity method to find further applications of independent interest. As an example, we give a quantum algorithm that learns SYK Hamiltonians from the Gibbs state at any constant temperature with polynomial time and sample complexity.
summary: This paper introduces a rigorous quantum cavity method to develop polynomial-time classical and quantum algorithms for mean-field models. It successfully estimates thermal expectations for both classical spin glasses (Ising model) and quantum systems (SYK model) up to their respective phase transitions. This work provides significant algorithmic advances for analyzing strongly correlated and disordered quantum matter.
main_problem: The central problem is developing polynomial-time classical and quantum algorithms to estimate local thermal expectations for mean-field models, especially in regimes approaching a glass transition.
main_result: The authors prove polynomial-time classical algorithms for estimating thermal expectations in the Ising p-spin model up to its glass transition, and for the SYK model at any constant temperature. They also provide a quantum algorithm to learn the SYK Hamiltonian from the Gibbs state.
method: The primary technique is the development and application of a rigorous quantum cavity method, which allows for the control of expectations and concentration around the saddle point in the thermodynamic limit.
model_or_system: The work focuses on mean-field models, specifically the classical Ising p-spin model (exhibiting spin glass behavior) and the quantum Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, both characterized by dense random interactions.
key_observables: Local thermal expectations of operators (e.g., spin expectations for Ising, $	ext{Tr}(\mathcal{O} e^{- eta H}) / 	ext{Tr}(e^{- eta H})$ for SYK).
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), system size ($N$), and the critical temperature/transition point ($ eta^*$ or any constant $ eta > 0$).
main_assumptions: The classical algorithms rely on the assumption that typical instances concentrate around the saddle point, and the quantum cavity method requires establishing factorization properties to control errors.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the classical prediction of thermal observables for the SYK model, comparing results across different system sizes and increasing Hermite degree, showing convergence to the infinite-$N$ prediction.
paper_structure: The paper develops the quantum cavity method to rigorously control expectations in mean-field models. It applies this method first to the classical Ising model to solve the open question of computing expectations up to the glass transition, and then to the quantum SYK model for calculating thermal expectations and learning its Hamiltonian.
why_interesting: The development of the quantum cavity method provides a powerful, rigorous tool for analyzing complex, highly interacting quantum systems like SYK, bridging the gap between mean-field theory and exact results in a way that is applicable to quantum information and many-body physics.
